sub_sections.title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
sub_sections.content:
## 2.1 Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

### The career logic of FIELDWISE

FIELDWISE is designed around a single, coherent career transition. The fellow enters the action as a plant physiologist and agronomist and leaves it as an Earth-observation and geospatial crop scientist able to work independently on transferable agricultural intelligence. The intended progression is explicit: Plant Physiologist/Agronomist to EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist to Independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. Every training and supervision measure below is aligned to that trajectory, so that skills development is not a generic add-on but the mechanism by which the fellowship changes what kind of researcher — and employee — the fellow becomes. The action is a European Fellowship of 30 months, comprising a 24-month research period hosted at ELTE followed by a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR that supplies the inter-sectoral half of the profile. This structure is deliberate: the academic host builds the scientific and methodological competences, and the non-academic placement builds the operational and sector-facing competences that the host cannot provide, so that the resulting profile is credible both inside and outside academia.

### Skills development: the competence gap and how it is closed

The skills-development plan starts from an honest statement of where the fellow is strong and where she is not. She combines a foundation in agronomy, plant protection and plant physiology with developing expertise in EO, GIS and agricultural data science. FIELDWISE addresses the remaining, well-identified competence gap in Bayesian and probabilistic modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty quantification, domain adaptation and decision evaluation. Because the gap is named precisely, the training content can be matched to it precisely rather than promised in the abstract.

The host-to-fellow training content is correspondingly specific. Through supervised research practice and named ELTE courses the fellow acquires: geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning and domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software and web deployment; and IP and research exploitation. These eleven competences are delivered as supervised practice plus named ELTE courses and are written into the Career Development Plan as concrete training and career needs, not as aspirations. They are exactly the competences the scientific work packages consume, so the fellow learns them by doing the science the proposal is funded to do — the strongest form of postdoctoral skills acquisition.

Critically, the transfer of knowledge is genuinely two-way rather than a one-directional upskilling. The fellow brings to ELTE plant physiology, horticultural crop science, plant protection and agronomy, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping, hyperspectral field measurement, the biological interpretation of Earth-observation signals, and preliminary development of the DrR - Digital Agronomist concept. This bidirectionality — crop physiology and agronomy in exchange for geospatial and data science — is what makes the fellow a bridging researcher at the end of the action rather than a physiologist who has taken some machine-learning courses. It is also the basis of a distinctive and defensible scientific profile: biological understanding combined with scalable geospatial prediction and operational agricultural decision support, a combination that is scarce in either community alone.

Beyond the eleven research competences, the plan develops seven transferable-skill strands: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. These are the competences an independent researcher needs to lead rather than to assist, and they are the competences employers outside academia value as much as inside it. Open science is embedded in the day-to-day work — harmonisation protocols, validation split manifests, hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, analysis and model code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata and open-access publication — so FAIR and open-science literacy are practised on real project outputs rather than taught in isolation.

### Supervision and quality assurance as a development instrument

The supervision arrangements are structured to make skills acquisition monitored and correctable. There is a weekly one-to-one meeting between the fellow and the supervisor, and a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor through the modelling-intensive work packages WP3 (Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction) and WP4 (Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability), tapering to monthly outside that window. A monthly written progress record is held by the fellow, and there is a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors. The co-supervisor provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing, while the fellow designs, builds and runs the models — a division that gives the fellow ownership of the scientific method while ensuring the newest and most demanding competences (probabilistic modelling, uncertainty, validation design) are quality-assured by an expert. This is credible mentoring for exactly the part of the profile that is new to her.

### The Career Development Plan as the carrying instrument

All of the above is made operational, trackable and reviewable through the Career Development Plan (deliverable D1.3, Career Development Plan), owned jointly by the fellow and the supervisor and established jointly by both supervisors and the fellow. It is an early deliverable, agreed by M3, and it carries six components: research objectives (O1 to O6); training and career needs (the eleven host-to-fellow competences delivered as supervised practice plus named ELTE courses); the seven transferable-skill strands; teaching; publications planning; and open-science engagement. It is not a one-off document: it is reviewed at each of the five steering points across the action, and its progress is itself a tracked key performance indicator — the plan is to be agreed by M3 and reviewed at all five steering points. Attaching a KPI to the plan means the fellow's development is governed with the same discipline as the scientific deliverables, which is what an evaluator needs to see to believe the career measures are real rather than declaratory. The review point that falls within the placement period ensures that non-academic career development is actively reviewed at precisely the moment it is most in play.

### Employability inside academia

The scientific competences the fellowship builds are directly matched to academic and research-sector demand. By the end of the action the fellow will hold advanced competence in Bayesian and probabilistic modelling, uncertainty quantification, spatio-temporal validation, sensor-domain transfer, cross-country adaptation, operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and IP and exploitation, together with the experience of taking a scientific concept the full length of the pipeline — from experimental evidence to a validated model, to cross-country testing, to commercial-field testing, to a delivered MVP. Very few early-career researchers can demonstrate that end-to-end span. This profile is relevant to European research institutes, universities, EU agricultural and environmental research, and Earth-observation organisations. The teaching measures reinforce the academic track specifically: the fellow co-designs and delivers a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, and co-supervises the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. Teaching is framed not as a competence to be acquired but as an existing strength transferred into a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction — the fellow taught for five years at university level, including syllabus design, lecturing and examining and Bachelor's thesis supervision — with the developmental step being the move to Earth-observation teaching in English at an informatics faculty and the step up from Bachelor's to doctoral-level supervision. This gives the fellow demonstrable, current higher-education teaching experience at the host, which is a concrete asset for an academic appointment.

Publication planning is aligned to the same end. Dissemination targets four principal scientific outputs — physiological and hyperspectral early-warning signatures of processing-tomato water stress; hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling; temporal and cross-country transferability of water-stress models; and research-to-commercial transfer and decision-oriented evaluation of agricultural AI — with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions targeted during or shortly after the fellowship. A first-author publication record on a distinctive topic is the currency of academic progression, and the plan builds it deliberately.

### Employability outside academia

The non-academic placement at AgroVIR is the measure that makes the beyond-academia claim credible rather than asserted. AgroVIR is the non-academic placement host, and the six-month placement is embedded inside the company that operates the commercial farms the project targets. The placement supplies the inter-sectoral half of the career progression — operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and direct exposure to commercial agricultural software requirements — none of which the academic host can provide. It is precisely the segment of the profile that makes the fellow employable in precision-agriculture companies, irrigation-technology companies and farm-management-information-system (FMIS) providers, as well as in academia. The placement work content is deliberately training-oriented rather than service to the company: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; a structured operational assessment of the MVP; authoring an FMIS integration roadmap from inside an implementing company; and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. Each of these is a transferable, sector-recognised competence. The placement is supervised on site by a named senior member of the company's research staff, giving the inter-sectoral training the same mentoring seriousness as the academic period. Because the placement is assessed by evaluators as part of Part B-1, it is presented here as an integral career measure and not merely as a scheduling detail: it converts the fellow's operational-transfer competences from a claim into lived, evidenced experience.

### Contribution of the proposed skills development to the future career

Taken together, the measures produce a researcher whose profile spans a genuine gap in the European research and innovation landscape. The academic period builds the scientific and methodological depth; the placement builds the operational and inter-sectoral breadth; the Career Development Plan governs and reviews both; and the two-way knowledge transfer ensures the fellow ends as a bridging scientist rather than a specialist in one camp. This is a direct instantiation of the MSCA-PF expected outcome of an increased set of research and transferable skills and competences leading to improved employability and career prospects within academia and beyond (EO-01), and of the associated impact of improved researcher employability and career mobility within and beyond academia (EI-01). The international dimension (the Hungary-to-Bulgaria transfer work with MVCRI), the inter-sectoral dimension (the AgroVIR evaluation and placement) and the interdisciplinary dimension (the physiology-to-geoinformatics transfer) also forge the new mind-sets and cross-boundary approaches the programme seeks (EO-02). The credibility of the career case rests on three features an evaluator can check: the competence gap is named precisely and the training is matched to it; the plan carries a tracked KPI and five review points, so development is governed, not merely promised; and the inter-sectoral claim is backed by a real, six-month placement inside a commercial company rather than by assertion. On this basis the proposed measures are well suited to enhancing the fellow's career perspectives and employability across both academic and non-academic destinations.

sub_sections.title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
sub_sections.content:
## 2.2 Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

### Design logic: measures matched to a single-fellow action

FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship carried by one experienced researcher hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), with three associated partners (MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR) and a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR at the end of the 30-month action. The dissemination, exploitation and communication plan is therefore deliberately proportionate to what one fellow can deliver: every measure is anchored to a named project output or a named activity that already sits in the work plan, and none is promised beyond the resources of a single fellowship. Two design commitments run through the whole plan. First, project outputs are handled on the principle "as open as possible, as closed as necessary", so that openness is the default and closure is the justified exception rather than the reverse. Second, each impact route is carried by a tracked key performance indicator drawn from the confirmed set K1 to K11, so that the plan can be verified rather than merely asserted. This sub-section also discharges a specific commitment made in response to the previous evaluation of an earlier submission, which criticised that the economic and technological route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated; the exploitation route and the IP treatment below are the direct answer to that criticism.

### Dissemination to scientific audiences

Scientific dissemination targets four principal scientific outputs: physiological and hyperspectral early-warning signatures of processing-tomato water stress; hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling for water-stress prediction; temporal and cross-country transferability of agricultural water-stress models; and research-to-commercial transfer and decision-oriented evaluation of agricultural AI. At least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions are targeted during or shortly following the fellowship, with at least one open-access article per project year. The primary target group for these outputs is the agricultural remote-sensing and plant-physiology research community — Earth-observation-for-agriculture scientists and hyperspectral proximal-sensing researchers — for whom the physiology-to-satellite bridge is the novel contribution.

Beyond publications, dissemination is carried by the release of concrete, reusable research assets. The Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2) is released with documented transferability verdicts — every candidate hyperspectral feature carrying an explicit transferable or hyperspectral-only verdict (KPI K2) — and the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2) is released with a published model card (KPI K4). These are aimed at European research organisations and precision-agriculture model developers seeking reusable transfer features and forecasting engines. The Hungary→Bulgaria transferability report (D4.2) and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), which states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to move the model to a new agro-environment (KPI K6), are shared with the international partner MVCRI and the wider Bulgarian and Hungarian processing-tomato research and advisory community. The Harmonised historical database (D1.1), due in month 6, is curated to be FAIR with documented QC flags and metadata (KPI K1). Consistent with the Horizon Europe and MSCA open-science requirements the call sets out, the expected open outputs include harmonisation protocols, validation split manifests, the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, analysis and model code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata, selected derived or anonymised datasets and open-access publications, with data management planned to Horizon Europe open-science standards. Together these measures advance the expected outcomes on enhanced networking and knowledge transfer (EO-07) and the corresponding impact on increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations (EI-05).

### Communication and public engagement

Communication reaches beyond scientific peers to processing-tomato growers and farm advisors working with AgroVIR, and to the interested general agricultural public. Two concrete measures serve this group: one public field demonstration of the web MVP with AgroVIR farmers, and one public-facing article per project year. These measures were adopted specifically to address the expected impact on broadened public engagement with research and innovation (EI-03) and the expected outcome on enhanced networking and communication capacities with peers and with the general public (EO-03); the draft addresses neither of these on its own, so the measures are recorded honestly as operator-decided activities that carry no deliverable identifier rather than being attached to a fabricated deliverable. Science communication is one of the seven transferable-skill strands of the Career Development Plan set out in sub-section 2.1 and is not repeated here. Research results are also fed back into higher education through the co-design and delivery of a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, and the co-supervision of the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work — measures that serve the expected outcome on regular feedback of research results into teaching (EO-08) and the impact on enhanced integration of research results into teaching at host organisations (EI-06).

### Exploitation: from validated research to an operational route

Exploitation converts the science into a usable capability while remaining honest about how far a fellowship can carry it. The desktop research prototype is advanced to a scientifically validated DrR web MVP (D5.1), delivered by month 24 and serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution (KPI K7). The MVP is then externally evaluated by AgroVIR through the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4), which covers all nine assessment dimensions (KPI K9) and, together with the Field Decision Value report (D5.3, KPI K8), supplies evidence about whether the technology meets actual agricultural software requirements and whether it delivers field-level decision value under commercial farming conditions. The transferable assets — the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2), the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2) and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3) — are packaged for reuse by other agro-environments beyond the Hungary and Bulgaria test cases. The exploitation chain terminates in the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5), delivered in month 30, which names the required interfaces and the post-fellowship steps needed to embed FIELDWISE outputs into farm management information systems (KPI K10). This gives the project a research-to-operation delivery path with a named post-MSCA FMIS integration route (outcome OC5). The exploitation plan is deliberately bounded: the MVP is the research-to-operation demonstrator, not the primary scientific objective, and full commercial integration is not promised within the fellowship. The six-month AgroVIR placement is what makes this operational-transfer half structural rather than asserted, because the operational hardening, the nine-dimension assessment and the roadmap all depend on the company's own production environment and customer-facing requirements. These measures carry the scientific, technological and European impacts of the project (IMP-SCI, IMP-TECH, IMP-EU) and strengthen international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary collaboration (EI-02).

### Sustainability beyond the fellowship

The plan includes concrete actions that persist after the action ends. The released predictive engine with its model card (D3.2) and the Harmonised historical database (D1.1) remain maintained, FAIR research outputs held at ELTE; the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2) and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3) provide a documented, reusable method — with a stated minimum local-calibration cost — for transferring the approach to further crops and regions; the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5), grounded in AgroVIR's external evaluation, defines the post-fellowship steps required to move the validated web MVP toward operational use; and the co-designed ELTE MSc module unit embeds the project's methods into ongoing higher-education teaching. Responsibility for sustaining these outputs is shared across ELTE, MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR.

### Management of intellectual property and protection measures

As a single-beneficiary MSCA postdoctoral fellowship, FIELDWISE carries no bespoke consortium IP arithmetic, and the default position applies: results are owned by the host, ELTE, with the fellow as author-inventor, and open dissemination of scientific results — open-access publications, the released transfer library and the published model card — is the primary route to impact. Protection measures are proportionate and are invoked only where they are warranted. Where the web MVP or the predictive engine has commercialisation potential, protection would rely primarily on copyright in the software and on trade secrets around calibration data, with formal patenting considered only if the AgroVIR evaluation identifies protectable, novel technical subject matter. Access to and use of MVCRI and AgroVIR data are governed by the partners' agreed access conditions; commercially sensitive farmer data — yields, irrigation records and field geometries from AgroVIR farms — are handled under a data-sharing agreement and results are published only in aggregated or anonymised form. A specific background-IP boundary is managed explicitly: the DrR - Digital Agronomist components are the fellow's background IP, and the placement was structured as training-oriented work (operational hardening of the prediction pipeline, a structured operational assessment, authoring the FMIS integration roadmap from inside the implementing company, and requirements engineering and user testing with growers) rather than the development of the fellow's own prototype inside a commercial partner, precisely to keep the ownership boundary clean. The ownership of any results generated during the placement is to be settled by written agreement between the fellow, ELTE and AgroVIR; this arrangement is identified as a point to be formalised before the placement begins. This IP treatment, together with the AgroVIR-evaluated route to users, is the substantive answer to the previous evaluation's criticism that the economic and technological route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated.

### Contribution to expected outcomes and impacts

Taken together, the measures form a coherent, verifiable and proportionate pathway to impact for a single fellowship: open, peer-reviewed dissemination and reusable released assets serve knowledge transfer among European research organisations (EO-07, EI-05); public demonstration and annual public-facing articles broaden engagement with research (EO-03, EI-03); teaching integration feeds results into higher education (EO-08, EI-06); the externally evaluated web MVP and the named FMIS integration route give the science an operational and inter-sectoral destination (EI-02, and the technological and European impacts of the project); and the IP treatment protects value without closing off the open-science route that is the fellowship's primary impact mechanism. Each route carries a tracked KPI and terminates in a named deliverable or a stated activity, so an evaluator can check that every claimed outcome has a concrete measure behind it, delivered during the action and sustained after it.

sub_sections.title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
sub_sections.content:
## 2.3 The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

### What magnitude means for a single-fellow action

FIELDWISE is a 30-month European Fellowship carried by one experienced researcher hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), with MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR as associated partners. Its contribution to impact is therefore stated at the scale a fellowship can credibly reach and no further: not a deployed commercial product, but a validated method, a set of reusable research assets, and an evidenced route to users — each of which is deliberately designed to matter beyond the immediate crop (processing tomato) and the immediate geography (Hungary and Bulgaria). The magnitude of the contribution is expressed here through two honest devices: reach and reusability (what the outputs let others do after the action), and quantified project evidence rather than advance promises (what the project will actually measure). This sub-section does not restate the career measures of sub-section 2.1 or the dissemination, exploitation and communication mechanisms of sub-section 2.2; it argues why the results make a difference, and how large that difference credibly is.

### Scientific impact: reframing how agricultural AI is judged, and building assets that outlast the action

The project's central scientific contribution is to provide a framework for agricultural AI evaluated according to temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy, and to establish a methodological bridge between high-information proximal hyperspectral observations and scalable Sentinel-based prediction (project impact IMP-SCI). The importance of this reaches well beyond FIELDWISE, because agricultural machine learning is predominantly evaluated through retrospective metrics such as R², RMSE and F1-score, which can produce optimistic performance estimates that are unsuitable for actual irrigation management. Reframing the evaluation question — from how accurately a model reproduces the past to whether its signal survives across seasons, across countries and into commercial fields, and whether it arrives early enough to change a decision — addresses a field-wide weakness rather than a project-specific one.

That scientific contribution is not left as an argument; it is embodied in concrete, reusable outputs that persist after the fellowship: the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2), which carries an explicit transferable or hyperspectral-only verdict for every candidate feature (KPI K2); the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2), released with a published model card (KPI K4); and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), which states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to move the model to a new agro-environment (KPI K6). The Adaptation protocol is the mechanism that scales the scientific contribution past its immediate scope: because the cost of adapting the method to a new setting is stated rather than left implicit, the approach becomes portable to further crops and regions beyond processing tomato and beyond the Hungary-to-Bulgaria pair. In magnitude terms, the project therefore delivers not a single trained model but a documented, transferable method with a known adaptation cost — a contribution to increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations, and, through the physiology-to-geoinformatics bridge, to the spread of interdisciplinary approaches in the European R&I culture.

### Societal, environmental and agricultural impact: a large problem where better timing matters

The societal importance of the work follows from the scale of the problem it addresses. Approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, while climate change is expected to intensify drought frequency and severity and to increase both the agricultural area requiring irrigation and irrigation demand in already irrigated areas. Water scarcity already translates into agricultural yield losses and higher water costs (project impact IMP-AGRI). Against a problem of that magnitude, even modest improvements in the timing and spatial prioritisation of irrigation carry substantial agronomic, economic and environmental relevance, and processing tomato — whose productivity depends strongly on the temporal interaction between water availability, atmospheric demand and developmental stage — is a demanding, high-value test case in which those improvements can be demonstrated.

The environmental contribution (IMP-ENV) is stated with deliberate discipline. FIELDWISE contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings in irrigated agriculture by improving irrigation timing and prioritisation, but the project does not claim in advance that it will achieve a particular percentage reduction; impact is to be quantified from project evidence. That evidence is generated by the Field Decision Value report (D5.3), which computes decision value for at least two competing models and reports warning lead time, false-action rate and missed-stress rate (KPI K8). This is what makes the magnitude claim credible rather than promotional: the size of the environmental and agricultural benefit is measured against what the models actually deliver in decision terms, not asserted as a headline number the fellowship cannot yet support.

### Economic and technological impact: from prototype to a validated demonstrator with a named route to scale

The economic and technological contribution is to advance the work from a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated DrR web MVP (D5.1), delivered by month 24 and serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution (KPI K7), and to subject that MVP to external, inter-sectoral scrutiny through the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4), which covers all nine assessment dimensions (KPI K9). This external evaluation is the source of the project's evidence about whether the resulting technology meets actual agricultural software requirements (IMP-TECH) — evidence that a single academic actor cannot generate alone, and which raises the importance of the contribution from a research artefact to a technology assessed under operational expectations.

The route by which this contribution can scale beyond the action is named rather than left open: the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5), delivered in month 30, states the required interfaces and the post-fellowship steps needed to embed FIELDWISE outputs into farm management information systems (KPI K10), giving the project a research-to-operation delivery path with a named post-MSCA integration route (outcome OC5). The economic magnitude of that route is indicated by the reach of the channel it targets: AgroVIR operates a farm management information system in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria — the potential integration surface into which the roadmap is written, even though deployment itself is explicitly not promised within the fellowship. At the European level (IMP-EU), the MATE-MVCRI architecture directly investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment can be transferred to another, contributing to a wider European question — how locally developed agricultural intelligence can become reliably transferable rather than remaining confined to the field in which it was trained — that bears on the competitiveness and knowledge-transfer capacity of European research organisations and on the strength of international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary collaboration.

### Honest bounding, and why it strengthens the magnitude case

The magnitude of the contribution is bounded truthfully. The web MVP is the research-to-operation demonstrator, not the primary scientific objective, and full commercial integration is not promised within the fellowship; no advance numeric target is set for water saving. These limits are not concessions but the reason the impact case is believable: the project claims exactly what its outputs and KPIs can evidence — a transferability-first evaluation framework, three reusable and documented assets, a validated and externally assessed demonstrator, and a named integration route — and each impact route (scientific, environmental and agricultural, technological, and European) terminates in a named deliverable and a tracked KPI. An evaluator can therefore check the size of every claimed contribution against a concrete, measurable output, which is what distinguishes a genuine contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts from an aspirational one.

The Harmonised historical database (D1.1), due in month 6, is curated FAIR with QC flags and metadata (KPI K1).

Communication to growers, advisors and the general public comprises one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year; an operator measure carrying no deliverable id, mapped to EI-03/EO-03.

Research results feed into teaching via a co-designed ELTE MSc module unit on Earth observation for agriculture and co-supervision of one PhD student's field-experiment component, mapped to EO-08/EI-06.

The MVP is externally evaluated by the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4, nine dimensions, KPI K9) alongside the Field Decision Value report (D5.3, KPI K8).
The FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5), delivered in month 30, names required interfaces and post-fellowship steps (KPI K10), giving a named post-MSCA FMIS integration route (OC5).
The MVP is the research-to-operation demonstrator, not the primary scientific objective, and full commercial integration is not promised within the fellowship.

Results persist beyond the fellowship as maintained FAIR outputs at ELTE, a reusable transfer library and adaptation protocol, the FMIS roadmap, and the embedded MSc module, shared across ELTE, MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR.

The IP strategy is the MSCA default: results owned by ELTE with the fellow as author-inventor; open dissemination as primary route; protection via software copyright and trade secrets on calibration data; patenting only if the AgroVIR evaluation identifies protectable novel subject matter; partner data under agreed access conditions.
Commercially sensitive AgroVIR farm data are governed by a data-sharing agreement and published only in aggregated or anonymised form.

The DrR - Digital Agronomist components are the fellow's background IP, and the placement was structured as training-oriented work rather than development of her own prototype inside the company to keep the ownership boundary clean.
Ownership of results generated during the placement is a point to be formalised by written agreement between the fellow, ELTE and AgroVIR before the placement begins.
The exploitation route and IP treatment answer the previous evaluation's criticism that the economic/technological route to users and IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated.
Measures are proportionate to a single-fellow action, each anchored to a named output or activity, delivered during the action and sustained after it, with each route carrying a tracked KPI (K1-K11).
The dissemination, communication and exploitation measures map to Tier 2B expected outcomes and impacts (EO-03, EO-07, EO-08; EI-02, EI-03, EI-05, EI-06).
FIELDWISE is a 30-month action.
The action is a European Fellowship.
The fellowship is hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE).
MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR are associated partners of the action.

The project provides a framework for agricultural AI evaluated by temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy, and a methodological bridge between proximal hyperspectral observations and Sentinel-based prediction.
Agricultural ML is predominantly evaluated through retrospective metrics (R2, RMSE, F1-score) that can produce optimistic and operationally misleading performance estimates.
The Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2) carries an explicit transferable or hyperspectral-only verdict for every candidate feature (K2).
The FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2) is released with a published model card (K4).
The Adaptation protocol (D4.3) states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to move the model to a new agro-environment (K6).
Because D4.3 states an adaptation cost, the method is portable to further crops and regions beyond processing tomato and the Hungary-to-Bulgaria pair.

The scientific contribution and reusable assets advance increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations and the spread of interdisciplinary approaches (EI-05, EI-02).
Approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, with climate change intensifying drought and irrigation demand.

Water scarcity already produces yield losses and higher water costs while irrigation demand rises; processing tomato is a high-value test case where improved timing has substantial agronomic and economic relevance.

The project contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings by improving irrigation timing and prioritisation and makes no advance percentage claim; impact is quantified from project evidence.
The Field Decision Value report (D5.3) computes decision value for at least two competing models with lead time, false-action rate and missed-stress rate reported (K8).

The project advances from a desktop prototype to a validated DrR web MVP (D5.1, month 24, K7) externally evaluated by the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4) across nine assessment dimensions (K9), giving evidence on whether the technology meets actual agricultural software requirements.
The FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5, month 30) names required interfaces and post-fellowship steps (K10), giving a research-to-operation path with a named post-MSCA integration route (OC5).

No participation in EU-funded research projects. AgroVIR's relevant track record is commercial rather than scientific: twenty years of practice in Hungarian commercial agriculture, and a farm management information system in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria — the two countries FIELDWISE works in.

The MATE-MVCRI architecture investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment transfers to another, contributing to the wider European question of transferable agricultural intelligence.
The web MVP is the research-to-operation demonstrator, not the primary scientific objective, and full commercial integration is not promised within the fellowship.
Each impact route terminates in a named deliverable and a tracked KPI, so the size of every claimed contribution is checkable.
